one_liner: CMake 3.16+ target_precompile_headers: parses a shared header set once per target instead of once per source file.
what_it_does: A CMake command, target_precompile_headers(<target> PRIVATE|PUBLIC|INTERFACE <headers>...), that writes a generated cmake_pch.h/.hxx listing the headers, compiles it once into a .gch/.pch artifact and force-includes it into every source of the target (-include for GCC, /Yc, /Yu and /FI for MSVC, -include-pch for Clang), so sources need no #include "pch.h". A second form, target_precompile_headers(<target> REUSE_FROM <other>), lets targets with identical flags share one PCH artifact. It is a build-system switch, not a library: a few CMakeLists.txt lines, no source edits.
how_it_is_fast: Precompiled headers: the compiler front end preprocesses, parses and analyses the listed headers once and serialises that state to disk; each translation unit loads the image instead of re-parsing the same STL, Qt or Boost headers. The gain scales with the share of each TU's front-end time spent in the shared headers. For Clang 11+ (not AppleClang) CMake also passes -fpch-instantiate-templates by default (PCH_INSTANTIATE_TEMPLATES, CMake 3.19), so template instantiations are done once while building the PCH.
when_to_use: Header-heavy C++ targets where many sources include the same stable, expensive headers (STL, Qt, Boost, windows.h, a large in-house framework) and front-end parsing dominates compile time.

MSVC and clang-cl builds on Windows: the only published CMake numbers (the implementer's 2019 Qt Creator run) show 37.28% with Visual C++ 2017 and 30.66% with Clang-cl 8.0.0 against 22.09% with MinGW GCC 8.1.0.

Clang 18+ builds: LLVM's own CMake now enables target_precompile_headers by default for Clang 18 and newer (and disables it for GCC), and an LLVM RFC reported 1.5-2x faster LLVM builds (search snippet only; the thread was unreachable).
Groups of targets with identical compile flags (test executables, plugins) that can share one PCH through REUSE_FROM, so the header set is compiled once for all of them.
Replacing a hand-maintained stdafx.h/pch.h scheme or the cotire module with a generator-independent, built-in mechanism.
when_not_to_use: GCC builds: LLVM's HandleLLVMOptions.cmake turns PCH off by default with GCC because, tested with GCC 14 and 15, it gave very little compile-time improvement while substantially increasing build-directory size.

Headers that change often: the PCH is force-included into every source of the target, so editing any precompiled header rebuilds the PCH and recompiles the whole target (and every target reusing it); headers used by only one or two sources add cost without benefit.

Builds behind sccache, or ccache with non-Clang compilers: LLVM disables PCH there by default because sccache does not support PCH and ccache can return stale objects when only a macro definition changes (ccache issue 1668, sccache issues 615 and 2562); clang-cache and C++20-modules builds are excluded too.

Very large header sets: llvm-project issue 61750 reports a PCH built from mlpack.hpp taking 190 s and 7.8 GB to build with Clang 17 and making an empty int main() take 90 s and 4.1 GB to compile (open, no diagnosis).
Installed or exported library targets: CMake's docs say to avoid PUBLIC/INTERFACE precompile headers there (or wrap them in $<BUILD_INTERFACE:...>), because consumers should choose their own PCH.

integration.form: build-system feature (CMake command and target properties; nothing to link)
integration.dependencies: CMake 3.16+ and a compiler with PCH support (GCC, Clang/AppleClang, MSVC, clang-cl)
integration.min_toolchain: CMake 3.16 (PCH_WARN_INVALID 3.18, PCH_INSTANTIATE_TEMPLATES 3.19 with Clang 11+, ALIAS targets 4.5, PCH_WARNINGS in the 4.6 docs on master)
integration.platforms: Any CMake platform with GCC (.gch), Clang/AppleClang (.pch) or MSVC/clang-cl (.pch with /Yc and /Yu); Xcode and FASTBuild generators have their own code paths; multi-arch Apple builds get one PCH per architecture
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — no source changes are needed, but every source now sees the precompiled headers force-included, which can mask missing #includes and introduce name collisions (per the LLVM RFC), and Objective-C/C++ or other-language files may need SKIP_PRECOMPILE_HEADERS

gotchas: CMake marks the generated PCH header as a system header (#pragma GCC/clang system_header), so warnings from the precompiled headers silently disappear; the PCH_WARNINGS property (4.6 docs) restores them, and LLVM clears the undocumented CMAKE_PCH_PROLOGUE for the same reason (CMake issue 21219).

REUSE_FROM requires identical compile options, flags and definitions on both targets; if they differ the compiler may be unable to use the PCH, and with GCC only the -Winvalid-pch warning (on by default through PCH_WARN_INVALID since 3.18) reports it. LLVM disables reuse for targets with non-default RTTI/EH or with C sources.

Compiler caches need extra flags: LLVM adds -Xclang -fno-pch-timestamp for Clang and -fpch-preprocess for GCC so ccache can cache PCH builds, and enables ccache depend mode when PCH is on (llvm-project PR 225118).
PCH artifacts are per language: Objective-C (.m) and Objective-C++ (.mm) files in C/C++ targets can fail to compile with Ninja/Makefile generators until marked SKIP_PRECOMPILE_HEADERS.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick PCH when a single machine's clean or CI build is dominated by re-parsing the same headers and you want a gain without a cache server or build farm; it keeps one translation unit per source, so unlike the sibling CMake unity-build entry it adds no ODR clashes and keeps incremental rebuilds fine-grained. It complements rather than replaces sccache/ccache, distcc/icecream or FASTBuild, but check the cache-compatibility caveats before combining it with sccache or with ccache on GCC/MSVC.
verified_claims_summary: The only CMake-specific timings are the implementer's 2019 Qt blog post (unreachable here; figures from search summaries): a CMake build of Qt Creator on one Windows 10 Ryzen machine, using the pre-release MR 3553 code, was 22.09% faster with MinGW GCC 8.1.0, 37.28% with Visual C++ 2017 and 30.66% with Clang-cl 8.0.0 than the same build without PCH. If these are time saved, as the same author's unity-build MR figures are, they equal about 1.28x, 1.59x and 1.44x (derived from page data); there is no CPU model, flags, run count or benchmark code.
